item.title: Marginalized and Misunderstood: The Outer Edges of Columbine
item.description:
Adverse Childhood Experiences

Marginalized and Misunderstood: The Outer Edges of Columbine

Unmasking facades and addressing teen trauma early can avert catastrophe.

Posted October 7, 2026

Key points
  • Critical warning signs were dismissed due to suburban privilege and compliant public facades.
  • Media scapegoating silenced innocent students and deepened survivor guilt after the tragedy.
  • Journaling and owning her narrative empowered survivor Krista Hanley to heal from long-term trauma.
  • Stopping youth violence requires confronting teen despair and providing early psychiatric care.
Reclaiming her narrative: Columbine survivor Krista Hanley turns past trauma into empowerment and advocacy.
Source: Canva / Used with permission

The 1999 Columbine High School shooting became a generation-defining American tragedy. But for Krista Hanley, who walked into the school that spring morning as an innocent junior student, it was not a national talking point. It was an event she survived.1

Sitting down with Krista decades later, one is struck not by the shadow of that day, but by the quiet luminescence of her presence. Decades later, Krista radiates warmth and quiet strength, having reclaimed her story free of bitterness.

Krista states that only when she reached the safety of home and watched the news footage did the shattering truth register: The perpetrators were not nameless “monsters” who had invaded from the outside, but two boys she knew from her circle of friends—Dylan Klebold and Eric Harris.2

Coping With Trauma

Like so many who endure catastrophic violence, Krista found herself navigating an internal labyrinth of shock, grief, and survivor’s guilt.3 In the immediate aftermath, society often demands that survivors either disappear quietly back into normal life or immediately step up as neatly packaged symbols of resilience. Neither option leaves space for the raw, jagged reality of trauma.

Redemption began when Krista dared to own her narrative. Around 2012, she began unearthing her old high school journal, confronting the fragmented memories she had locked away for so long. Putting pen to paper transformed from an accidental exercise into a life-saving exercise. Writing allowed her brain to organize and process the senseless chaos, separate truth from media myth, and finally process her survivor’s guilt. By confronting the full, complicated reality of Columbine—neither excusing the horrific violence nor sanitizing the deep cultural failures that preceded it— Krista found the strength to rebuild her sense of agency and step out of the shadows.

Media Misrepresentation of the "Trench Coat Mafia"

In the frantic media frenzy that followed, a convenient scapegoat was born overnight: the so-called “Trench Coat Mafia.” Headlines mischaracterized Krista’s small group of friends as an organized, sinister cabal that supposedly marched down the hallways exchanging Nazi salutes.4 The reality was far more mundane, yet profoundly heartbreaking. The name itself had originated as a harmless inside joke among a loose gathering of eight to ten marginalized, disenfranchised teenagers. Krista recalls, “We were not an ideological syndicate; we were simply outsiders navigating the brutal social hierarchy of a 1990’s suburban high school.” Like many schools, Columbine's culture centered on athletes and cheerleaders with privileged status. “Those of us who dressed in black dusters, smoked cigarettes, or refused to conform were instantly pushed to the periphery, cast as troublemakers, and subjected to routine bullying,” remembers Krista. The group was Krista and her friends' refuge—a fragile harbor where kids who felt invisible and alienated could find solidarity.

Within that misunderstood haven, Dylan and Eric were familiar, everyday fixtures. Like so many seventeen-year-old girls, Krista viewed them through the uncomplicated lens of a high school crush. To Krista’s young eyes, Dylan was quiet, tall, and stoic—an intelligent, depressed wallflower whom she would deliberately cross paths with in the hallways just to catch a nod of acknowledgment. Eric was gregarious, fast-talking, and restless, always trying to carve out a presence that never quite seemed comfortable. Krista spent weekends with Dylan, Eric, and friends, dreading life with expectations after graduation.

Missed Warning Signs

Krista recalls that clear warning signs were missed. According to David Cullen, about a year before the attack, Dylan and Eric were arrested for breaking into a parked van to steal computer gear.4 Despite the serious crime, their suburban privilege secured them a juvenile diversion program over harsher sentencing. Articulate and privileged, they completed community service early with glowing reviews. Society looked away, mistaking a desperate cry for help as harmless mischief.

Beneath suburban normalcy, Dylan secretly journaled about self-hatred, untreated depression, and suicide, while Eric was prescribed antidepressants for his explosive anger—clear warning signs left unresolved.

A year earlier, other warning signs surfaced: Their violent essays and home videos targeted the school, the symbol of their perceived abandonment and oppression. They sought to eliminate the school building—both the physical structure and the symbol of their perceived abandonment and oppression. Yet school administrators barely recognized these warning signs before sweeping them under the rug.

Two days before the attack, the contrast between their turmoil and public facade peaked. Both Dylan and Eric attended the school's festive After Prom party. Krista spent hours gaming and talking with them and hugged them goodbye. They were skilled at presenting the compliant faces expected of them by teachers, parents, and friends. Their true objective was total annihilation—detonating massive cafeteria propane bombs, not just a shooting. The school symbolized their rage, repression, and perceived powerlessness. Aiming for catastrophic destruction, their violence exposed the deadly endpoint of untreated depression, resentment, and isolation.

Aftermath: Shame, Guilt, and Silencing Survivors

When the dust settled, the tragedy left Krista and others who survived in a secondary prison of shame. Because Krista had escaped physically uninjured, and because she was associated with the teenage group the national media had villainized, she felt stripped of her right to grieve. Society demanded easy villains, creating guilt by association that silenced her entire community. Terrified of blame or exposure, Krista swallowed and buried her trauma. Fearing condemnation, she abandoned her writing dreams. For a decade, unprocessed trauma left her emotionally untethered and fearful.

Krista Hanley’s Work in Violence Prevention

Today, Krista’s perspective is grounded in a deep commitment to meaningful action and violence prevention. Through her writing and work running a business that teaches personal safety and self-defense skills, Krista empowers others to trust their intuition, establish boundaries, and take command of their physical and emotional spaces. True prevention requires looking beyond denial, checklists, and the illusion that privilege shields youth from mental distress. Preventing violence requires unmasking facades and providing early psychiatric care. Overcoming trauma means turning pain into empathy, courage, and action.

In the end, one is left with a haunting question: Could this catastrophe have been averted if we had simply dared to listen, set aside judgment, and truly face the dark, intricate labyrinth of teenage despair before it exploded into unfathomable ruin?

item.title: 5 Active Listening Skills to Build Stronger Friendships
item.description:
Friends

5 Active Listening Skills to Build Stronger Friendships

Learn to listen in ways that make friends feel seen, heard, and valued.

Posted October 7, 2026

Key points
  • Active, distraction-free listening enhances connection.
  • Open-ended questions can spark deeper conversations.
  • Giving others the time and space to talk builds trust.

Listening just might be the magic key for building friendships. We need those keys more than ever, as loneliness is still affecting a majority of college students.

According to Dr. Vivek H. Murthy, “Loneliness and isolation represent profound threats to our health and well-being. But we have the power to respond.”

Source: Mia Nosanow

One of the best ways to respond to loneliness is building the skill of listening to each other. Attentive listening facilitates awareness, understanding, and empathy.

1. Check Your Body Language

Our body language conveys the quality of our listening. Having an open face and body shows others that you are available. Make eye contact if possible. Turn your body toward the person you are listening to. Notice if your arms are crossed, creating a physical barrier between you and the other person. If it feels authentic, nod and gesture to convey that you are listening.

2. Put the Phone Away

It needs to be said: Phone use gets in the way of authentic listening. If you look down at your phone and send a quick text, you have told the person you are talking to that they do not command your full attention. If you intend to have a deep conversation and listen closely, put your phone on silent and put it away.

3. Ask Open-Ended Questions

Open-ended questions reflect your own curiosity and intention to learn about the other person. They are invitations for the person to share their thoughts and ideas, to reflect more deeply and broadly. Open-ended questions usually start with how, what, or why.

4. Reflect Back What Others Say

From time to time, restate or clarify what you have heard the other person say. This lets the other person know that they have been heard correctly and prevents you from misunderstanding. Reflecting back is only about confirming your understanding, not giving your opinion or being judgmental.

Source: Mia Nosanow

5. Remember to WAIT

In general, but especially when your intention is to listen deeply, avoid giving advice or expressing your opinion unless the person expressly requests it. A good acronym to remember is WAIT, which stands for “Why am I talking?” We all want to jump in and help solve a situation or connect the situation to our own experience. Those aren’t bad impulses, but be patient and don’t rush in or interrupt the person. Sometimes, the best thing we can do is to allow others to have time and space to express themselves so they can figure out a solution for themselves.

When to Seek Professional Help

If you are struggling to listen to people, for any reason, consider seeking help, whether from a counselor, clergy, or a trusted mentor. Struggling to listen to others could be a symptom of many issues that can be hard to tease apart, such as anxiety, attention-deficit disorder, autism issues, or depression.

Listening can be hard. It takes courage to be truly present with someone and want to hear their truth. Yes we want to share about ourselves, but we need to keep it balanced and also learn about the other person. This will help us connect more deeply and fight the loneliness that is so present for many of us.

To find a therapist, visit the Psychology Today Therapy Directory.
